chapters.n: The date is precise: late summer of 520 BC, under the Persian king Darius I. The Jews had returned from Babylon about 18 years earlier, but the temple still lay unfinished. Haggai speaks to the governor and high priest.

f.g: Darius I of Persia, who reigned 522–486 BC.
Governor of Judah, a grandson of King Jehoiachin — a descendant of David.
The high priest, also called Jeshua (Ezra 3:2).

chapters.n: The people were saying, “It’s not the right time to build the Lord’s house.” Opposition and hard times had stalled the work since about 536 BC.
God’s answer comes through His prophet.
A pointed question: Is it time for you to live in nicely paneled houses while My house lies in ruins? Their priorities were upside down.

f.g: Paneled houses — finished with fine wood, a sign of comfort.

chapters.n: “Consider your ways” — think carefully about what you’re doing and what it’s producing. Haggai repeats this call several times.

f.g: Literally “set your heart on your ways.”

chapters.n: They work hard but never get ahead: big plantings, small harvests; never enough food or warmth; wages leaking out like coins from a bag with holes. Neglecting God left them empty.

f.w: Ye have sown much, and bring in little

chapters.n: Again God urges them to reflect honestly on their choices.
The solution is simple: go to the hills, bring timber, and build. God will be pleased and glorified in it.

f.g: Or “I will show My glory.”

chapters.n: They hoped for much but got little, and God blew it away. Why? Because they rushed to their own houses while His lay in ruins.

f.g: Blew it away like chaff.

f.w: ye run every man unto his own house

chapters.n: That’s why the sky has held back dew and the land its crops. The drought was a message.

f.g: Withheld dew — vital moisture in Israel’s dry summers.

chapters.n: God called a drought on grain, wine, oil, people, animals, and all their work. Everything they depended on suffered.

f.g: Hebrew ḥoreb — a wordplay with ḥareb, “waste” (v. 4, 9): a wasted house brings a dry land.

chapters.n: The leaders and the people obeyed the Lord’s voice through Haggai, and they reverenced the Lord. A rare and quick response to a prophet!

f.w: obeyed the voice of the LORD

f.g: Those who had returned from exile.

chapters.n: Haggai, the Lord’s messenger, brings a short but powerful promise: “I am with you.”
The Lord stirred up the spirit of the governor, high priest, and people, and they began working on the temple. God gives energy to those who obey.

f.w: the LORD stirred up the spirit

chapters.n: Work began just 23 days after Haggai’s first message — September 520 BC. Obedience was swift.

f.w: the four and twentieth day of the sixth month
f.g: About September 21, 520 BC.

chapters.n: A second message comes about seven weeks later, during the Feast of Tabernacles (October 520 BC) — the same feast when Solomon had dedicated the first temple.

f.w: the seventh month, in the one and twentieth day
f.g: The last day of the Feast of Tabernacles; about October 17, 520 BC.

chapters.n: Again the message is for the governor, the high priest, and all the people.

f.g: The rest — the returned remnant.

chapters.n: Some older people remembered Solomon’s glorious temple, destroyed 66 years earlier. Compared to it, this new building seemed like nothing, and they were discouraged.

f.w: Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory?

chapters.n: God’s answer: Be strong, Zerubbabel; be strong, Joshua; be strong, all you people — and work, for I am with you. The same encouragement God gave Joshua of old.
God’s covenant from the Exodus still stands, and His Spirit remains among them. Don’t be afraid.
In a little while God will shake heaven, earth, sea, and land. Hebrews applies this “shaking” to the removal of all that is temporary so the unshakable kingdom remains.

f.w: I will shake the heavens, and the earth

chapters.n: He will shake all nations, and their treasures will come in, and He will fill this house with glory. Many Christians read “the desire of all nations” as the Messiah, who came to this temple.

f.g: Hebrew can mean “the treasures of all nations”; many Christians also see it as pointing to Christ.

f.w: I will fill this house with glory

chapters.n: The silver and gold belong to God anyway. If He wants the temple beautified, He has the resources.

f.w: The silver is mine, and the gold is mine

chapters.n: This later temple’s glory will be greater than Solomon’s, and here God will give peace. The Savior Himself would later teach in this temple (as rebuilt by Herod).

f.w: The glory of this latter house shall be greater
in this place will I give peace

chapters.n: A third message comes two months later, in December 520 BC.

f.w: the four and twentieth day of the ninth month
f.g: About December 18, 520 BC.

chapters.n: Haggai poses a question about the law to the priests, whose job was to teach it.

f.w: Ask now the priests concerning the law

chapters.n: If someone carries holy sacrificial meat in a fold of his robe and touches other food, does holiness spread to it? The priests answer, “No.”

f.g: Meat consecrated as a sacrifice.
The fold or hem of a garment.

chapters.n: But if someone unclean from touching a dead body touches food, does it become unclean? “Yes.” Uncleanness spreads easily; holiness doesn’t transfer by contact.
Haggai’s point: the people themselves had been “unclean” through neglect, so even their offerings were unclean. Rebuilding the altar alone didn’t make them holy; their hearts needed to change.

f.w: that which they offer there is unclean

chapters.n: Now think back to how things were before the temple foundation stones were laid.

f.g: Set your heart — think carefully.

chapters.n: Back then, a grain heap expected to hold twenty measures held only ten; a wine vat expected to yield fifty measures gave only twenty.

f.g: Wine vat.

chapters.n: God had struck their crops with blight, mildew, and hail, yet they didn’t turn to Him.
But consider this day — the day the temple foundation was laid again. Things are about to change.

f.w: the foundation of the LORD's temple was laid

chapters.n: The seed isn’t even harvested yet, and the trees haven’t borne fruit — but from this day on God will bless them. The promise comes before the evidence; they must trust it.

f.w: from this day will I bless you

chapters.n: A fourth message comes the same day, this one just for Zerubbabel.

f.w: the four and twentieth day of the month
f.g: The same day as verse 10.

chapters.n: God will shake the heavens and the earth.

f.w: I will shake the heavens and the earth

chapters.n: He will overturn the thrones of kingdoms and destroy their military power; armies will turn on each other — as at the Red Sea and in Gideon’s battle.

f.w: every one by the sword of his brother

chapters.n: God chooses Zerubbabel and makes him like a signet ring — a royal seal of authority. This reverses the curse on his grandfather Jehoiachin and keeps David’s line alive; Zerubbabel appears in Jesus’s genealogy.

f.g: A seal ring used to sign official documents — a symbol of royal authority.
